claim: The microtubule cytoskeleton is critical for muscle cell differentiation.
source: The microtubule cytoskeleton is critical for muscle cell differentiation and undergoes reorganisation into an array of paraxial microtubules, which serves as template for contractile sarcomere formation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Bischoff and Holtzer, 1968; Holtzer et al., 1975; Toyama et al., 1982) and is a foundational statement in the abstract.

claim: The microtubule cytoskeleton undergoes reorganisation into an array of paraxial microtubules during muscle cell differentiation.
source: The microtubule cytoskeleton is critical for muscle cell differentiation and undergoes reorganisation into an array of paraxial microtubules, which serves as template for contractile sarcomere formation.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Warren, 1974) and is a well-established observation in the field.

claim: The paraxial microtubule array serves as a template for contractile sarcomere formation.
source: The microtubule cytoskeleton is critical for muscle cell differentiation and undergoes reorganisation into an array of paraxial microtubules, which serves as template for contractile sarcomere formation.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Antin et al., 1981; Pizon et al., 2005) and represents established knowledge.

claim: oMAP4 is a previously uncharacterised isoform of microtubule-associated protein MAP4.
source: In this study, we identify a previously uncharacterised isoform of microtubule-associated protein MAP4, oMAP4, as a microtubule organising factor that is crucial for myogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RT-PCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 2.

claim: oMAP4 is a microtubule organising factor that is crucial for myogenesis.
source: In this study, we identify a previously uncharacterised isoform of microtubule-associated protein MAP4, oMAP4, as a microtubule organising factor that is crucial for myogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by depletion experiments showing defects in cell elongation, fusion, and microtubule organization (Figures 2, 3).

claim: oMAP4 is expressed upon muscle cell differentiation.
source: We show that oMAP4 is expressed upon muscle cell differentiation and is the only MAP4 isoform essential for normal progression of the myogenic differentiation programme.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and Western blot data showing upregulation after 24 hr of differentiation (Figure 2B, C).

claim: oMAP4 is the only MAP4 isoform essential for normal progression of the myogenic differentiation programme.
source: We show that oMAP4 is expressed upon muscle cell differentiation and is the only MAP4 isoform essential for normal progression of the myogenic differentiation programme.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experiments showing that only oMAP4 depletion causes significant defects in differentiation markers and cell morphology (Figures 2, 3).

claim: Depletion of oMAP4 impairs cell elongation.
source: Depletion of oMAP4 impairs cell elongation and cell–cell fusion.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements showing oMAP4-depleted cells are significantly shorter (82 ± 39 μm vs 107 ± 40 μm for control) (Figure 2E, F).

claim: Depletion of oMAP4 impairs cell-cell fusion.
source: Depletion of oMAP4 impairs cell elongation and cell–cell fusion.
evidence: This is supported by fusion efficiency data showing more than fourfold reduction in oMAP4-depleted cells (Figure 2G).

claim: oMAP4 is required for paraxial microtubule organisation in muscle cells.
source: Most notably, oMAP4 is required for paraxial microtubule organisation in muscle cells and prevents dynein- and kinesin-driven microtubule–microtubule sliding.
evidence: This is supported by manual tracing and EB3 tracking data showing reduced microtubule alignment in oMAP4-depleted cells (Figure 3G-L).

claim: oMAP4 prevents dynein- and kinesin-driven microtubule-microtubule sliding.
source: Most notably, oMAP4 is required for paraxial microtubule organisation in muscle cells and prevents dynein- and kinesin-driven microtubule–microtubule sliding.
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation experiments showing increased microtubule sliding frequency and velocity in oMAP4-depleted cells (Figure 4A-D).

claim: Purified oMAP4 aligns dynamic microtubules into antiparallel bundles in vitro.
source: Purified oMAP4 aligns dynamic microtubules into antiparallel bundles that withstand motor forces in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy experiments showing preferential zippering of antiparallel microtubules (Figure 6A-C).

claim: oMAP4-mediated microtubule bundles withstand motor forces in vitro.
source: Purified oMAP4 aligns dynamic microtubules into antiparallel bundles that withstand motor forces in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by kinesin gliding assays showing that >75% of oMAP4-bundled microtubules resist motor-driven separation (Figure 7C, E, F).

claim: Microtubule organisation changes from a radial, centrosome-dominated array in undifferentiated cells to a paraxial array in myotubes.
source: As reported previously, we found that microtubule organisation changes from a radial, centrosome-dominated array in undifferentiated cells, to a paraxial array in myotubes (Figure 1A) (Warren, 1974; Tassin et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by structured illumination microscopy images in Figure 1A and citations to prior work.

claim: The asymmetry in the distribution of microtubule growth angles increases significantly during the first two days of differentiation.
source: The asymmetry in the distribution of microtubule growth angles increases significantly during the first two days of differentiation (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by EB3 tracking data showing increased Kuiper statistics over time (Figure 1B-D).

claim: Guided growth of microtubules contributes to the progressively more ordered parallel microtubule array in differentiating cells.
source: This suggests that guided growth of microtubules (probably along existing microtubules) contributes to the progressively more ordered parallel microtubule array in differentiating cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increasing asymmetry in microtubule growth angles during differentiation.

claim: Microtubules within the array are highly motile in undifferentiated myoblasts.
source: Furthermore, microtubules within the array are highly motile in undifferentiated myoblasts as visualised by the photoactivation of paGFP-Tubulin or conversion of mEos2-Tubulin (Figure 1E,F, Videos 1, 2).
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation experiments showing frequent microtubule sliding events in undifferentiated cells (Figure 1E-H).

claim: In differentiating muscle cells, microtubules become very stable and static.
source: In differentiating muscle cells, microtubules become very stable and static as seen by the low frequency and speed of microtubule-sliding movements and by diminished loss of microtubules from the photoactivated region due to depolymerisation (Figure 1E–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation data showing reduced sliding frequency and velocity in differentiated cells (Figure 1E-H).

claim: Conventional kinesin and dynein contribute to microtubule movements in myoblasts.
source: Both motors contribute to microtubule movements in myoblasts as the frequency of microtubule movements was reduced more than threefold upon depletion of either dynein heavy chain or Kif5b (Figure 1E–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Videos 4, 5).
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation experiments in motor-depleted cells showing reduced microtubule sliding (Figure 1E-H).

claim: Kif5b and dynein are continuously expressed during muscle differentiation.
source: However, Kif5b and dynein were continuously expressed during muscle differentiation (Figure 1I), suggesting that other factors prevent motor-dependent microtubule sliding and promote parallel microtubule array formation during myogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing constant protein levels across differentiation time course (Figure 1I).

claim: Other factors prevent motor-dependent microtubule sliding and promote parallel microtubule array formation during myogenesis.
source: However, Kif5b and dynein were continuously expressed during muscle differentiation (Figure 1I), suggesting that other factors prevent motor-dependent microtubule sliding and promote parallel microtubule array formation during myogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that motor expression remains constant while microtubule motility decreases during differentiation.

claim: Mouse skeletal muscle cells express tissue-specific isoforms of MAP4.
source: Mouse skeletal muscle cells express tissue-specific isoforms of MAP4 (Mangan and Olmsted, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The ubiquitous isoform uMAP4 is continuously expressed during C2C12 differentiation.
source: We confirmed the continuous expression of the ubiquitous isoform uMAP4 and upregulation of muscle-specific mMAP4 24 hr post induction of differentiation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 2B.

claim: Muscle-specific mMAP4 is upregulated 24 hr post induction of differentiation.
source: We confirmed the continuous expression of the ubiquitous isoform uMAP4 and upregulation of muscle-specific mMAP4 24 hr post induction of differentiation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data in Figure 2B.

claim: oMAP4 has a unique 48 kD projection domain.
source: Interestingly, we found that a previously uncharacterised isoform, with a unique 48 kD projection domain, was also upregulated after 24 hr of differentiation.
evidence: This is based on the predicted molecular weight from the cDNA sequence and domain structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: oMAP4 is upregulated after 24 hr of differentiation.
source: Interestingly, we found that a previously uncharacterised isoform, with a unique 48 kD projection domain, was also upregulated after 24 hr of differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and Western blot data in Figure 2B-D.

claim: oMAP4 is highly expressed in brain tissue in addition to muscle.
source: In addition to muscle, this isoform is also highly expressed in brain tissue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of Affymetrix exon array data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: uMAP4, mMAP4, and oMAP4 transcripts are each expressed as variants with three, four, or five tau-like microtubule binding repeats.
source: Further analysis revealed that uMAP4, mMAP4, and oMAP4 transcripts were each expressed as variants with three, four, or five tau-like microtubule binding repeats due to alternative splicing of exons 14 and 15 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and restriction digest analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The variants with different numbers of microtubule binding repeats arise due to alternative splicing of exons 14 and 15.
source: Further analysis revealed that uMAP4, mMAP4, and oMAP4 transcripts were each expressed as variants with three, four, or five tau-like microtubule binding repeats due to alternative splicing of exons 14 and 15 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by restriction digest analysis showing presence/absence of specific exons in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: mMAP4 and oMAP4 protein levels increase between 24 and 48 hr after differentiation.
source: Both mMAP4 and oMAP4 protein levels increase between 24 and 48 hr after differentiation (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data in Figure 2C, D.

claim: GFP-fusion proteins of uMAP4, mMAP4, and oMAP4 decorate microtubules along their length in C2C12 cells.
source: As expected, GFP-fusion proteins of uMAP4, mMAP4, and oMAP4 decorated microtubules along their length in C2C12 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Depletion of uMAP4 does not significantly affect myoblast elongation.
source: Depletion of uMAP4 did not significantly affect this (105 ± 36 μm, p = 0.4; Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by cell length measurements in Figure 2E, F.

claim: Depletion of mMAP4 allows myoblasts to elongate to an average length of 143 ± 58 μm, which is significantly longer than control cells.
source: Depletion of mMAP4 allowed myoblasts to elongate to an average length of 143 ± 58 μm, which is significantly longer than control cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell length measurements in Figure 2E, F.

claim: Myoblast fusion efficiency is not significantly affected following the depletion of uMAP4 or mMAP4.
source: Myoblast fusion efficiency was not significantly affected following the depletion of uMAP4 or mMAP4 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by fusion analysis data in Figure 2G.

claim: oMAP4-depleted cells have an average length of 82 ± 39 μm, which is significantly shorter than control myoblasts.
source: oMAP4-depleted cells had an average length of 82 ± 39 μm, which is significantly shorter than control myoblasts (p << 0.001, Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by cell length measurements in Figure 2E, F.

claim: Cell-cell fusion efficiency is reduced more than fourfold following depletion of oMAP4.
source: Furthermore, cell–cell fusion efficiency was reduced more than fourfold following depletion of oMAP4 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by fusion analysis data in Figure 2G.

claim: Co-transfection of an RNAi-resistant version of oMAP4 rescues the myoblast elongation and fusion defects caused by oMAP4 shRNA.
source: Importantly, co-transfection of an RNAi-resistant version of oMAP4 (FLAG-oMAP4RIP) rescued the myoblast elongation and fusion defects caused by oMAP4 shRNA (Figure 2H,I, Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 2H, I.

claim: Overexpression of uMAP4 is not able to rescue oMAP4-depletion phenotypes.
source: The overexpression of uMAP4 was not able to rescue oMAP4-depletion phenotypes (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 2I.

claim: oMAP4 is specifically required for morphogenesis and cell-cell fusion during muscle cell differentiation.
source: Our data collectively demonstrate that oMAP4 is specifically required for morphogenesis and cell–cell fusion during muscle cell differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined depletion and rescue experiments showing specific effects of oMAP4.

claim: There is a severe delay and reduction in the expression of embryonic myosin in oMAP4-depleted cells.
source: We find a severe delay and reduction in the expression of embryonic myosin, a structural protein required for sarcomere formation, in oMAP4-depleted cells (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data in Figure 3A-C.

claim: The relocation of centrosomal proteins to the nuclear surface of myoblasts is severely delayed in oMAP4-depleted cells.
source: Likewise, the relocation of centrosomal proteins to the nuclear surface of myoblasts, a characteristic event during myogenesis (Tassin et al., 1985; Srsen et al., 2009), is severely delayed in oMAP4-depleted cells (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by PCM-1 localization data in Figure 3D, E.

claim: Progression through the myogenic differentiation programme depends on oMAP4.
source: These results confirm that progression through the myogenic differentiation programme depends on oMAP4.
evidence: This is inferred from the delays in multiple differentiation markers upon oMAP4 depletion.

claim: Depletion of oMAP4 does not result in a reduction of tubulin acetylation.
source: Depletion of oMAP4 did not result in a reduction of tubulin acetylation (Figure 3F), perhaps because other microtubule stabilisers were still present.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification in Figure 3F.

claim: The microtubule cytoskeleton appears disorganised in oMAP4-depleted cells.
source: Nevertheless, the microtubule cytoskeleton appeared disorganised in oMAP4-depleted cells (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by visual inspection of microtubule organization in immunofluorescence images in Figure 3A, B.

claim: In control cells, approximately 80% of microtubules are oriented ±15° of the longitudinal cell axis.
source: We found that the microtubule network was largely parallel in control cells with ∼80% of microtubules oriented ±15° of the longitudinal cell axis.
evidence: This is supported by manual tracing data in Figure 3G, H.

claim: In oMAP4-depleted cells, paraxial microtubule alignment is reduced to approximately 50%.
source: This was reduced to ∼50% in oMAP4-depleted cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by manual tracing data in Figure 3G, H.

claim: Microtubule orientation is fully rescued by expression of an RNAi-resistant oMAP4 construct.
source: Microtubule orientation was fully rescued by expression of an RNAi-resistant oMAP4 construct (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by manual tracing data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Depletion of mMAP4 increases paraxial microtubule alignment.
source: Depletion of mMAP4 increased paraxial microtubule alignment and uMAP4 depletion slightly reduced it (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by manual tracing data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: uMAP4 depletion slightly reduces paraxial microtubule alignment.
source: Depletion of mMAP4 increased paraxial microtubule alignment and uMAP4 depletion slightly reduced it (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by manual tracing data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Microtubule growth speed and duration are only slightly affected by oMAP4 depletion.
source: While microtubule growth speed and duration were only slightly affected, the orientation of microtubule growth deviated more from the longitudinal cell axis when oMAP4 was depleted compared to control cells (Figure 3J–L, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by EB3 tracking data in Figure 3J-L.

claim: The orientation of microtubule growth deviates more from the longitudinal cell axis when oMAP4 is depleted compared to control cells.
source: While microtubule growth speed and duration were only slightly affected, the orientation of microtubule growth deviated more from the longitudinal cell axis when oMAP4 was depleted compared to control cells (Figure 3J–L, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by EB3 tracking data in Figure 3I-L.

claim: Depletion of oMAP4 results in a more than fourfold increase in the frequency of microtubule sliding events.
source: Depletion of oMAP4 resulted in a more than fourfold increase in the frequency of microtubule sliding events, and these were significantly faster than those in control cells (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation experiments in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Microtubule sliding events in oMAP4-depleted cells are significantly faster than those in control cells.
source: Depletion of oMAP4 resulted in a more than fourfold increase in the frequency of microtubule sliding events, and these were significantly faster than those in control cells (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation experiments in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Rare sliding events in differentiated control cells are usually restricted to movements parallel to the long axis of the cell.
source: In addition, the rare sliding events in differentiated control cells were usually restricted to movements parallel to the long axis of the cell, while microtubules were observed to loop in oMAP4-depleted cells, similarly to undifferentiated cells (Figure 4E, Videos 1–3, 10, 11).
evidence: This is supported by directionality analysis of microtubule movements in Figure 4E.

claim: Microtubules loop in oMAP4-depleted cells, similarly to undifferentiated cells.
source: In addition, the rare sliding events in differentiated control cells were usually restricted to movements parallel to the long axis of the cell, while microtubules were observed to loop in oMAP4-depleted cells, similarly to undifferentiated cells (Figure 4E, Videos 1–3, 10, 11).
evidence: This is supported by directionality analysis of microtubule movements in Figure 4E.

claim: oMAP4 acts to maintain the parallel microtubule network by restricting microtubule movement.
source: These observations suggest that oMAP4 acts to maintain the parallel microtubule network by restricting microtubule movement, especially those that are off-axis.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased microtubule motility and disorganization upon oMAP4 depletion.

claim: Depletion of dynein heavy chain alone does not significantly affect the already low-microtubule sliding frequencies in differentiated cells.
source: Depletion of dynein heavy chain alone did not significantly affect the already low-microtubule sliding frequencies in differentiated cells, although the velocity of microtubule sliding was reduced (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation experiments in dynein-depleted cells in Figure 4B-D.

claim: The velocity of microtubule sliding is reduced by dynein depletion.
source: Depletion of dynein heavy chain alone did not significantly affect the already low-microtubule sliding frequencies in differentiated cells, although the velocity of microtubule sliding was reduced (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation experiments in dynein-depleted cells in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Cells co-depleted for dynein and oMAP4 still show a high frequency of microtubule-sliding events.
source: Cells co-depleted for dynein and oMAP4 still showed a high frequency of microtubule-sliding events (Figure 4B,C), although fast sliding events and looping were reduced (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation experiments in double-depleted cells in Figure 4B-E.

claim: Fast sliding events and looping are reduced in cells co-depleted for dynein and oMAP4.
source: Cells co-depleted for dynein and oMAP4 still showed a high frequency of microtubule-sliding events (Figure 4B,C), although fast sliding events and looping were reduced (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is supported by photoactivation experiments in double-depleted cells in Figure 4D, E.

claim: Dynein co-depletion slightly alleviates the microtubule disorganisation caused by oMAP4 depletion, but does not fully rescue it.
source: Consequently, dynein co-depletion slightly alleviated the microtubule disorganisation caused by oMAP4 depletion, but did not fully rescue it (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by manual tracing data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: oMAP4 prevents microtubule sliding by crosslinking microtubules rather than by inhibiting dynein force generation per se.
source: These results suggest that oMAP4 prevents microtubule sliding by crosslinking microtubules rather than by inhibiting dynein force generation per se.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dynein co-depletion does not fully rescue oMAP4 depletion phenotypes.

claim: Expression of GFP-oMAP4 in undifferentiated myoblasts results in a significant increase in strong microtubule bundles.
source: Indeed, expression of GFP-oMAP4 in undifferentiated myoblasts resulted in a significant increase in strong microtubule bundles, while expression of GFP-uMAP4 had no effect (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of microtubule bundles in transfected cells in Figure 4F, G.

claim: Expression of GFP-uMAP4 has no effect on microtubule bundling in undifferentiated myoblasts.
source: Indeed, expression of GFP-oMAP4 in undifferentiated myoblasts resulted in a significant increase in strong microtubule bundles, while expression of GFP-uMAP4 had no effect (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of microtubule bundles in transfected cells in Figure 4F, G.

claim: Purified oMAP4 and GFP-oMAP4 have microtubule-binding activity.
source: Using in vitro microtubule co-sedimentation assays, we confirmed microtubule-binding activity of the purified proteins (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by co-sedimentation assay data in Figure 5B.

claim: When Taxol- or GMP-CPP-stabilised microtubules are incubated with 60-nM oMAP4, microtubule bundles and structures with crossovers are frequently observed.
source: When Taxol- or GMP-CPP-stabilised microtubules were incubated with 60-nM oMAP4, we frequently observed microtubule bundles and structures with crossovers (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy images in Figure 5C-F.

claim: oMAP4 has microtubule cross-linking activity.
source: This confirmed that oMAP4 has microtubule cross-linking activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of microtubule bundles and crossovers in the presence of oMAP4.

claim: The addition of GFP-oMAP4 promotes zippering of growing microtubules that encounter each other at shallow angles.
source: The addition of GFP-oMAP4 promoted zippering of those growing microtubules that encountered each other at shallow angles (Figure 6A–C; Video 13).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy observations in Figure 6A-C.

claim: No microtubule-zippering events are observed at angles between 25° and 150°.
source: No microtubule-zippering events were observed at angles between 25° and 150°, suggesting that oMAP4 can only generate forces to bend microtubules by up to 30°.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of zippering events relative to encounter angle in Figure 6B.

claim: oMAP4 can only generate forces to bend microtubules by up to 30°.
source: No microtubule-zippering events were observed at angles between 25° and 150°, suggesting that oMAP4 can only generate forces to bend microtubules by up to 30°.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of zippering at angles between 25° and 150°.

claim: oMAP4 shows a strong preference for zippering antiparallel-oriented microtubules.
source: Furthermore, oMAP4 showed a strong preference for zippering antiparallel-oriented microtubules (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of zippering events showing higher frequency for antiparallel encounters in Figure 6B.

claim: PRC1 is more potent to bundle-stabilised microtubules free in solution than oMAP4.
source: We observed that PRC1 was more potent to bundle-stabilised microtubules free in solution than oMAP4 (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by comparative bundling assays in Figure 5E, F.

claim: PRC1 is not able to zipper microtubules in assays using dynamic microtubules growing from immobilised seeds.
source: However, PRC1 was not able to zipper microtubules in our assays using dynamic microtubules growing from immobilised seeds (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data in Figure 6B.

claim: There is no substantial enrichment of GFP-oMAP4 in antiparallel or parallel overlaps.
source: We do not observe a substantial enrichment of GFP-oMAP4 in antiparallel or parallel overlaps (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on visual inspection of GFP-oMAP4 localization in Figure 6C.

claim: There is no difference in microtubule length between parallel and antiparallel encounters that result in zippering.
source: Likewise, there was no difference between parallel and antiparallel encounters that were zippered (p = 0.59) and those that did not result in zippering (p = 0.88) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microtubule length measurements in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: oMAP4 is a microtubule-organising factor that can arrange microtubules into antiparallel and with lesser efficiency parallel bundles.
source: Therefore, our results demonstrate that oMAP4 is a microtubule-organising factor, which can arrange microtubules into antiparallel and with lesser efficiency parallel bundles.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro zippering data showing preferential antiparallel bundling.

claim: oMAP4's function is consistent with the depletion phenotypes observed in differentiating muscle cells.
source: This function is consistent with the depletion phenotypes observed in differentiating muscle cells, where oMAP4 helps to arrange paraxial microtubules and thereby supports cell differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined in vitro and cellular data.

claim: Proteins of the MAP2/tau family are highly elongated, structurally disordered monomers.
source: Proteins of the MAP2/tau family are highly elongated, structurally disordered monomers (Hernandez et al., 1986; Devred et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: oMAP4, uMAP4, and tau share a similar structure of over 60% random coil, about 20% helical, and 13% extended strand.
source: Using the GOR secondary structure prediction method, we find that oMAP4, uMAP4, and tau share a similar structure of over 60% random coil, about 20% helical, and 13% extended strand (Garnier et al., 1996).
evidence: This is based on computational secondary structure prediction.

claim: No significant coiled-coil domain is predicted in oMAP4.
source: Furthermore, no significant coiled-coil domain was predicted.
evidence: This is based on computational structure prediction.

claim: oMAP4 has sedimentation constants of 3.6 ± 0.25 S and GFP-oMAP4 has 4.3 ± 0.21 S.
source: We obtained sedimentation constants of 3.6 ± 0.25 S and 4.3 ± 0.21 S, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by glycerol gradient sedimentation data in Figure 6D, E.

claim: oMAP4 is a highly elongated monomer with a frictional ratio ƒ/ƒmin = 2.1.
source: Given the molecular weight of the monomers being 99 kD and 131 kD, respectively, we can calculate the frictional ratio ƒ/ƒmin = 2.1, suggesting that oMAP4 is a highly elongated monomer with a shape comparable to tau (ƒ/ƒmin = 1.8, [Devred et al., 2004]).
evidence: This is calculated from the sedimentation data and molecular weight.

claim: oMAP4 most likely bundles microtubules using a second microtubule-binding region in its projection domain.
source: We, therefore, predict that oMAP4 most likely bundles microtubules using a second microtubule-binding region in its projection domain.
evidence: This is speculated based on the monomeric nature of oMAP4 and its bundling activity.

claim: The presence of 80 nM oMAP4 only slightly affects the velocity of kinesin-mediated movements of single microtubules.
source: The presence of 80 nM oMAP4 did only slightly affect the velocity of kinesin-mediated movements of single microtubules (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by kinesin gliding assay data in Figure 7A, B.

claim: Antiparallel-microtubule bundles formed in solution and landing on the kinesin surface are often static or their movement is slow and non-persistent.
source: However, antiparallel-microtubule bundles formed in solution and landing on the kinesin surface were often static or their movement was slow and non-persistent (Figure 7C–E, Video 14).
evidence: This is supported by kinesin gliding assay observations in Figure 7C-E.

claim: More than 75% of microtubule bundles withstand motor forces for the entire duration of 7.5 min videos.
source: Most importantly, we observed that more than 75% of microtubule bundles withstand motor forces for the entire duration of our 7.5 min videos (Figure 7C,E,F, yellow arrows), suggesting that oMAP4-mediated cross-linking is indeed able to prevent motor-driven microtubule sliding as we hypothesised.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of bundle resistance time in Figure 7F.

claim: oMAP4-mediated cross-linking is able to prevent motor-driven microtubule sliding.
source: Most importantly, we observed that more than 75% of microtubule bundles withstand motor forces for the entire duration of our 7.5 min videos (Figure 7C,E,F, yellow arrows), suggesting that oMAP4-mediated cross-linking is indeed able to prevent motor-driven microtubule sliding as we hypothesised.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most bundles resist motor forces.

claim: Microtubules fulfil a structural role during the elongation of muscle cells.
source: Our data support a model in which microtubules fulfil a structural role during the elongation of muscle cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between microtubule alignment and cell length.

claim: The degree of alignment of microtubules correlates with a cell's ability to elongate.
source: If so, one would expect that the degree of alignment of microtubules will correlate with a cell's ability to elongate. We tested this by plotting the Kuiper statistic as a measure of microtubule orderliness against the mean cell length of 48 hr differentiated cells for different RNAi treatments used in this study and found indeed a linear correlation (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by the linear correlation shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Myoblasts that fail to elongate are also impaired in cell-cell fusion.
source: As observed for oMAP4, our previously published data on EB3 depletion (Straube and Merdes, 2007) and a number of unpublished observations, myoblasts that fail to elongate are also impaired in cell–cell fusion.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple observations including oMAP4 depletion and prior EB3 depletion studies.

claim: oMAP4-depleted cells show a delay in the expression of myogenic markers in addition to impaired morphological changes.
source: oMAP4-depleted cells show in addition to impaired morphological changes, also a delay in the expression of myogenic markers, such as myogenin and embryonic myosin, further suggesting that a signalling step in the differentiation programme has not been completed.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A-C showing delayed marker expression.

claim: Dynein-mediated looping and buckling of microtubules brings microtubules into a favourable position for oMAP4-mediated zippering.
source: As oMAP4 is only able to efficiently zipper microtubules at incident angles of less than 30° if antiparallel and less than 10° if parallel, we propose that dynein-mediated looping and buckling of microtubules (Figure 4E; Fink and Steinberg, 2006; Tanenbaum et al., 2013) brings microtubules into a favourable position for oMAP4-mediated zippering.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the angle-dependence of oMAP4 zippering and known dynein activities.

claim: Dynein can only move those microtubules that are not yet aligned to the paraxial network because oMAP4-mediated bundling resists motor-driven sliding.
source: As oMAP4-mediated bundling resists motor-driven sliding, dynein can only move those microtubules that are not yet aligned to the paraxial network.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that oMAP4 bundles resist motor forces.

claim: Dynein and oMAP4 are likely to cooperate in the formation of the highly ordered microtubule arrangement in differentiating muscle cells.
source: Thus, dynein and oMAP4 are likely to cooperate in the formation of the highly ordered microtubule arrangement in differentiating muscle cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined effects of dynein and oMAP4 on microtubule organization.

claim: In the absence of oMAP4, excessive motor-driven microtubule motility disorganises microtubules.
source: In the absence of oMAP4, excessive motor-driven microtubule motility disorganises microtubules.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased microtubule motility and disorganization in oMAP4-depleted cells.

claim: In the absence of dynein, oMAP4 might stabilise high-angle microtubule crossovers but will not be able to align them into the network.
source: In the absence of dynein, oMAP4 might stabilise high-angle microtubule crossovers, but will not be able to align them into the network.
evidence: This is speculated based on the angle-dependence of oMAP4 zippering and the role of dynein in bringing microtubules together.

claim: If the activity of both oMAP4 and dynein is reduced, kinesin-mediated sliding and bundling prevails.
source: If the activity of both oMAP4 and dynein is reduced, oMAP4 zippering is missing and kinesin-mediated sliding and bundling (Straube et al., 2006; Jolly et al., 2010) prevails (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is speculated based on the known activities of kinesin and the effects of double depletion.

claim: Microtubule-microtubule sliding has been implicated in driving neurite outgrowth.
source: Microtubule–microtubule sliding has recently been implicated in driving neurite outgrowth (Lu et al., 2013), and paraxial microtubule arrangements have been shown to drive dorsal closure during embryonic development (Jankovics and Brunner, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Paraxial microtubule arrangements drive dorsal closure during embryonic development.
source: Microtubule–microtubule sliding has recently been implicated in driving neurite outgrowth (Lu et al., 2013), and paraxial microtubule arrangements have been shown to drive dorsal closure during embryonic development (Jankovics and Brunner, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The mechanisms of motor and MAP cooperation in the formation of paraxial microtubule networks are likely to be of importance beyond muscle cells.
source: Thus, the mechanisms we reveal here for motor and MAP cooperation in the formation of paraxial microtubule networks are likely to be of importance beyond muscle cells.
evidence: This is speculated based on the presence of paraxial arrays in other cell types.

claim: oMAP4 is highly expressed in brain.
source: Indeed, oMAP4 is highly expressed in brain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that it might be required to support the paraxial microtubule arrays in dendrites and the axon.
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: oMAP4 might be required to support the paraxial microtubule arrays in dendrites and the axon.
source: Indeed, oMAP4 is highly expressed in brain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that it might be required to support the paraxial microtubule arrays in dendrites and the axon.
evidence: This is speculated based on the high expression in brain and the known paraxial arrays in neurons.

claim: Symmetry breaking in cell migration occurs through protrusion mediated by the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Symmetry breaking in cell migration occurs through protrusion mediated by the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell migration.

claim: Microtubules support and stabilise cell protrusions.
source: Microtubules support and stabilise cell protrusions, and microtubule plus ends are selectively stabilised at the leading edge (Waterman-Storer et al., 1999; Kaverina and Straube, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Microtubule plus ends are selectively stabilised at the leading edge during cell migration.
source: Microtubules support and stabilise cell protrusions, and microtubule plus ends are selectively stabilised at the leading edge (Waterman-Storer et al., 1999; Kaverina and Straube, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In differentiating myoblasts, dynamic capture of microtubule plus ends occurs at the cell tips.
source: Similarly, in differentiating myoblasts dynamic capture of microtubule plus ends occurs at the cell tips (Straube and Merdes, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Dynamic capture of microtubule plus ends at cell tips leads to the selective stabilisation of paraxial microtubules to break the symmetry in the microtubule network.
source: This leads to the selective stabilisation of paraxial microtubules to break the symmetry in the microtubule network.
evidence: This is inferred from the known mechanism of microtubule capture at cell edges.

claim: The zippering mechanism promotes shorter microtubules to align to longer and already bundled microtubules and thus amplifies the directional bias and increases stability and orderliness in the paraxial array.
source: The zippering mechanism described here would promote shorter microtubules to align to longer and already bundled microtubules and thus amplify the directional bias and increase stability and orderliness in the paraxial array.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observed zippering activity of oMAP4.

claim: During myogenesis, microtubules are rearranged from a dynamic radial array to a parallel array of stable posttranslationally modified microtubules within the elongating cell.
source: During myogenesis, microtubules are rearranged from a dynamic radial array to a parallel array of stable posttranslationally modified microtubules within the elongating cell (Warren, 1974; Tassin et al., 1985; Saitoh et al., 1988; Gundersen et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Preventing detyrosination of tubulin or interfering with microtubule stabilisation by depletion of EB1 or MURF impairs expression of myogenic markers.
source: Preventing detyrosination of tubulin or interfering with microtubule stabilisation by depletion of EB1 or MURF impairs expression of myogenic markers (Spencer et al., 2000; Chang et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2009), thus suggesting that signalling through modified microtubules might control myogenic differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Signalling through modified microtubules might control myogenic differentiation.
source: Preventing detyrosination of tubulin or interfering with microtubule stabilisation by depletion of EB1 or MURF impairs expression of myogenic markers (Spencer et al., 2000; Chang et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2009), thus suggesting that signalling through modified microtubules might control myogenic differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that interfering with tubulin modifications affects differentiation markers.

claim: Changes in the regulation of microtubule dynamics at the cell cortex can result in cell polarisation and fusion defects without affecting the content of tubulin modifications or the expression of differentiation markers.
source: On the other hand, changes in the regulation of microtubule dynamics at the cell cortex that neither affect the content of tubulin modifications nor the expression of differentiation markers can result in cell polarisation and fusion defects as caused by the depletion of EB3 (Straube and Merdes, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on EB3 depletion.

claim: Microtubules have a dual function during the early stages of muscle cell differentiation to control morphological changes and biochemical composition.
source: This suggests a dual function of microtubules during the early stages of muscle cell differentiation to control (1) morphological changes and (2) biochemical composition, before later serving as structural templates for myofibrillogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the different types of defects observed upon various perturbations of the microtubule cytoskeleton.

claim: MAP2 and tau determine the spacing between microtubules in dendrites and axons, but do not control the directionality of microtubules within those bundles.
source: MAP2 and tau determine the spacing between microtubules in dendrites and axons, but do not control the directionality of microtubules within those bundles (Chen et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Proteins of the PRC1/MAP65/Ase1 family preferentially bundle microtubules in antiparallel orientation.
source: Proteins of the PRC1/MAP65/Ase1 family preferentially bundle microtubules in antiparallel orientation and are responsible for the stabilisation of the antiparallel microtubule overlaps in the spindle midzone during mitosis (Loiodice et al., 2005; Gaillard et al., 2008; Subramanian et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Microtubule-microtubule sliding by Eg5, kinesin-1, kinesin-14, and dynein has been implicated in microtubule organisation and force generation.
source: Microtubule–microtubule sliding by Eg5, kinesin-1, kinesin-14, and dynein has been implicated in microtubule organisation and force generation (Kapitein et al., 2005; Fink and Steinberg, 2006; Straube et al., 2006; Braun et al., 2009; Fink et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2013; Tanenbaum et al., 2013), and we begin to understand how the interplay of motors and MAPs organises particular microtubule arrangements (Janson et al., 2007; Bieling et al., 2010; Braun et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Upon differentiation, mono-nucleated myoblasts withdraw from the cell cycle and fuse to form syncytial myotubes.
source: Upon differentiation, mono-nucleated myoblasts withdraw from the cell cycle and fuse to form syncytial myotubes (Wakelam, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work and represents established knowledge.

claim: The microtubule cytoskeleton is required for myoblast differentiation and fusion.
source: The microtubule cytoskeleton is required for these processes (Bischoff and Holtzer, 1968; Holtzer et al., 1975; Toyama et al., 1982) and undergoes reorganisation into an array of paraxial microtubules (Warren, 1974), which serves as template for contractile sarcomere formation (Antin et al., 1981; Pizon et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.
